name: Urine therapy

card.summary: Drinking or applying urine for rejuvenation or skin; no evidence of benefit, with documented contamination concerns.
card.note: Medical sources report no demonstrated benefit and warn of risks; a looksmax.org user reported a negative experience.

quick.overview:
Urine therapy is an alternative-medicine practice in which a person drinks their own urine or applies it to the skin or gums for health or cosmetic purposes. It has traditional roots in several cultures and was popularised in modern times by the British naturopath John W. Armstrong in the 20th century.

In looksmaxxing forums it is discussed as a rejuvenation or skin practice, with proponents citing the idea that urine contains beneficial substances. A reference source states there is no scientific evidence of therapeutic benefit from untreated urine.
quick.mechanism: Proponents attribute effects to substances in urine, such as urea or claimed stem cells. Urine is over 95 percent water, and commercial urea creams use synthetic urea at concentrations far higher than urine provides.
quick.risks: Sources report no demonstrated benefit and note microbial contamination concerns. The American Cancer Society states that evidence does not support urine or urea helping cancer patients. One looksmax.org user posted a report of a negative experience drinking aged urine, describing a burning throat and nausea.

lead: Urine therapy, also called urotherapy, urinotherapy or shivambu, is an alternative-medicine practice that uses human urine for medicinal or cosmetic purposes, including drinking it and massaging it into skin or gums. In medieval hatha yoga a related practice was called amaroli.[1]

Medical and reference sources state there is no scientific evidence supporting claimed therapeutic benefits of untreated urine.[1] In looksmaxxing communities the practice appears mainly as a claimed rejuvenation or skin method, and at least one forum user has posted a first-person report of a negative experience.[2]
The term urotherapy is also used in paediatric urology for non-surgical bladder training and behavioural treatment; that use is unrelated to urine therapy as discussed here.

paras: Urine has appeared in traditional remedies across several systems, including 17th-century English medical texts and 19th- and early-20th-century remedy collections. Roman dentists reportedly used it to whiten teeth, and an early Islamic jurist permitted camel urine for medicinal purposes.[1]

British naturopath John W. Armstrong popularised drinking one's own urine in the early 20th century. He reportedly began prescribing it in 1918 and published The Water of Life: A Treatise on Urine Therapy in 1944.[1] Armstrong's book inspired the Indian work Manav Mootra (1959) by Raojibhai Manibhai Patel; medical anthropologist Joseph Alter has argued that modern Indian practice resembles Armstrong's version more than traditional Ayurveda or yoga.[1] Brief 1940s items titled Urine therapy appeared in the medical journals Experientia and The Medical Press.[3][4]

Proponents claim benefits for a wide range of conditions and for general health. Some practitioners claim anti-cancer effects, and some cancer clinics in Mexico have offered urotherapy alongside other alternative treatments.[1] Within looksmaxxing forums, a user guide describes urine therapy as a rejuvenation method, citing the idea that urine contains stem cells and other properties that proponents say rejuvenate the face.[2]

A 1971 NASA report found urine to be more than 95 percent water, with urea, chloride, sodium, potassium and creatinine as main solutes. Reference material states there is no scientific evidence of therapeutic use of untreated urine, and that the American Cancer Society says available evidence does not support urine or urea helping cancer patients.[1]

Commercial urea creams use synthetic urea at high concentrations as a humectant and keratolytic, whereas urine is too dilute for that purpose.[1] The belief that urine relieves jellyfish stings is also described as incorrect, with urination possibly worsening pain by triggering remaining stinging cells.[1] A 2010 study in the Pan African Medical Journal examined microbial contamination and public-health implications of urine used therapeutically in children.[1]

No studies found testing urine therapy for skin, appearance or rejuvenation. Research on urotherapy in paediatric urology concerns bladder and bowel training and is unrelated to drinking or applying urine.

A looksmax.org thread presents urine therapy as a rejuvenation practice, including the claim that fermenting or ageing urine increases stem cells. In the same thread the author reported a negative experience with drinking aged urine while sunbathing, describing a burning throat and nausea, and advised others against drinking aged urine.[2] Another user replied that the practice seemed excessive.[2]

timeline.event: John W. Armstrong reportedly begins prescribing auto-urine therapy.[1]
Armstrong publishes The Water of Life: A Treatise on Urine Therapy.[1]
Manav Mootra by Raojibhai Manibhai Patel appears in India.[1]
China's Ministry of Civil Affairs lists the Urine Therapy Association as an illegal organisation.[1]

lore.intro: Urine therapy is discussed in looksmaxxing forums as a fringe rejuvenation practice, with proponents' guides and at least one user warning from experience.[2]

claims.claim: Drinking or applying urine, especially aged urine, rejuvenates the face and skin.
claims.believers: A looksmax.org guide states that urine therapy practitioners report facial rejuvenation from urine's properties, including claimed stem cells, and that fermenting urine increases them.[2]
claims.experts: Reference sources report no scientific evidence of therapeutic use of untreated urine and note that urine is over 95 percent water, too dilute to act like commercial urea creams.[1]

claims.claim: Aged urine is safe to drink.
claims.believers: Proponents of fermenting urine claim it increases beneficial components; a user who tried it reported it burned his throat and caused nausea and advised others against drinking aged urine.[2]
claims.experts: A 2010 study examined microbial contamination and public-health implications of urine used therapeutically, and no studies show a benefit of drinking it.[1]

refs.title: Report. My negative experience on urine therapy. Never drink aged urine, it's harmful.
